Our client is Quillpath, a US software company. It sells cloud software that small home-services businesses — plumbers, landscapers, cleaners — use to schedule jobs, send quotes and get paid. Customers pay monthly and can cancel at any time. For years Quillpath sold one plan, Pro, at $100 a month. In January 2025 it launched a cheaper Starter plan at $40 a month, with fewer features and a single user. New customers per month nearly tripled. Quillpath's board has a rule: each type of customer should be worth at least three times what it costs to acquire. The CFO says Starter fails that test and wants to shut it down; the head of growth wants to keep it. The CEO has asked us what Quillpath should do with the Starter plan.

Feel free to take a moment — then talk me through how you'd approach it.

So I'd want to look at the market, the customer, the competition, and then the financials, and figure out whether Starter makes sense strategically. I'd probably also think about internal capabilities and maybe some risks around the brand. Then we'd land on a recommendation for the CEO.
Understood. That's a broad list of areas. Which one would you prioritize first for this decision, and why?
hmm, I'm not sure.
Take a moment if you need it. Coming back to your structure: which branch would you start with, and why?
I'm stuck, sorry.
No problem. Let's narrow it down. Let's move on: what data would you want to see first?

The board rule is a value-to-cost ratio, so I'd start with the two inputs for Starter. For value: $40 monthly price, gross margin, and how long a Starter customer stays — the monthly cancel rate. For cost: what Quillpath spends to acquire a Starter customer, sales and marketing divided by new Starter customers.

Do we have the churn rate and CAC for each plan?
A ratio-driven start. Here's an exhibit: Quillpath — Economics of each plan ($ per customer). With those figures, how would you put them together to test Starter against the board's three-times rule?

Pro's monthly gross margin is 100 − 20 = $80. Starter's is 40 − 10 = $20... sorry, that's wrong, it's $30.

Then LTV = margin × lifetime, and lifetime = 1 ÷ monthly cancel rate. To clear the 3x rule, Pro needs LTV ≥ $3,600, so lifetime ≥ 3,600/80 = 45 months, i.e. churn under about 2.2% a month. Starter needs LTV ≥ $900, so lifetime ≥ 900/30 = 30 months, churn under about 3.3% a month.

Do we have the monthly cancellation rate for each plan?

Got it. You've set the break-even churn for each plan. An exhibit for you — Customers who signed up in January–March 2025 — Status over their first year (% of each plan's starting customers, by months since sign-up). What does that tell you about whether each plan clears the board's three-times rule?

Pro: 78.5% left after 12 months → roughly 2% monthly cancel, so lifetime ≈ 50 months. LTV = 80 × 50 = $4,000 vs $1,200 CAC = 3.3x. Pro clears the rule.

Starter standalone: only 40% are still on Starter at month 12, but that 60% exit includes upgrades. 0.40 = (1−x)^12 → x ≈ 7.4% monthly exit from Starter, so about 13.5 months on plan × $30 = roughly $405 LTV. Against $300 CAC that's 1.35x — that's the CFO's number, and it fails.

But a fifth of Starter sign-ups upgrade to Pro and then behave like Pro customers. Using finance's own method: 20% × $4,000 = $800 extra per Starter sign-up. Total value ≈ $405 + $800 = $1,205, or 4.0x CAC — better than Pro.

So the CFO is measuring Starter as if it were a destination rather than partly a funnel.

Understood. You treated the 60% exit as one rate and then added the upgrade value separately. Starter's cancellations and its upgrades both count as leaving the plan. How did you separate them, so the upgrade value isn't counted twice or the Starter lifetime overstated?

I think it's consistent. The 7.4% is the combined exit rate — cancels plus upgrades — so 13.5 months is time spent paying $30 on Starter, nothing more. The Pro LTV I add on only covers the period after they switch, when they're paying $80. So no month gets counted twice.

The split within that exit is roughly 40 points cancelled, 20 points upgraded by month 12 — so about two-thirds of the leavers cancel outright, one-third upgrade. I applied the upgrade value to the 20% only, not the whole 60%.

One check I'd want: do we have the Pro-equivalent churn for upgraded customers? If upgraded customers churn faster than demo-sourced Pro customers, that $800 overstates it.

Mm-hm. As the exhibit shows: Cancellation rates have stayed roughly steady from month to month, very few Starter customers upgrade after month 12, upgraded customers then behave like Pro customers, and finance values a Starter sign-up at its Starter LTV plus one Pro LTV for each customer who upgrades. Of the 1,050 Pro customers who signed up in January–March 2025, 98.0% were still on Pro after month 1, 94.1% after month 3, 88.6% after month 6 and 78.5% after month 12, so 2.0%, 5.9%, 11.4% and 21.5% had cancelled by those months. Of the 3,000 Starter customers who signed up in January–March 2025, 94% were still on Starter after month 1, 82% after month 3, 65% after month 6 and 40% after month 12; by those months 1%, 5%, 11% and 20% had upgraded to Pro and were still customers, and 5%, 13%, 24% and 40% had cancelled. With that in hand, the Starter test is passed on the combined view. Before you take it to the CEO, what would you want to know about where those new Starter customers are coming from, and what that implies for Pro?

Cannibalization is the key risk. If a chunk of Starter sign-ups would have bought Pro at $100 anyway, we're trading a $4,000 customer for a $1,205 one — a $2,800 loss each time, even though Starter "passes."

The data I'd want: monthly new Pro sign-ups for, say, the 12 months before January 2025 versus the 12 months after. If Pro's run-rate held flat and total sign-ups tripled, Starter is genuinely incremental — new demand from smaller businesses who'd never pay $100. If Pro's volume fell after launch, the gap is cannibalization and I'd size it directly.

I'd also want the Starter sign-ups' business size — one-person shops versus multi-crew — since single-user firms were never Pro candidates. And whether Starter sign-ups ever requested a Pro demo first.

Do we have the Pro sign-up trend before and after January 2025?

Understood. Starter buyers are mostly one-person businesses, and Pro buyers mostly have three or more staff. Most Pro customers have a demo with a salesperson first, while Starter customers sign up online on their own. I have an exhibit for you: Quillpath — New customers per month, by plan (average per month). Given that, what does the Pro trend tell you about cannibalization, and how would you size its effect on the Starter decision?

Pro fell from 500 to 350 a month — 150 lost Pro sign-ups. Some of that could be market softness, but the self-serve/one-person profile says most Starter buyers are genuinely new, so I'll treat the 150 as cannibalized.

Sizing it per month. Value created by Starter: 1,000 × $1,205 ≈ $1.21m. Value lost: 150 Pro customers who would have been worth $4,000 each — but they didn't vanish, they bought Starter, so we recover $1,205 each. Net loss = 150 × ($4,000 − $1,205) = 150 × $2,795 ≈ $419k.

So net value added ≈ $1.21m − $419k ≈ $790k a month, roughly $9.5m a year. Starter is still clearly accretive.

I'd also note acquisition spend: Pro CAC is $1,200, so 150 fewer demos frees about $180k a month of sales cost — that's upside not in my number.
Right. You said a $2,800 loss each time Pro becomes Starter. How did you get that figure?

It's the gap between what a Pro customer is worth and what that same customer is worth once they buy Starter instead. Pro LTV is $4,000; a Starter sign-up is worth $1,205 all-in, including the chance they later upgrade. So $4,000 − $1,205 ≈ $2,795, rounded to $2,800. That's the value destroyed per cannibalized customer.

Strictly I should net off CAC too — we save $1,200 on the Pro acquisition and spend $300 on Starter, a $900 saving. So on a profit basis the loss is closer to $2,795 − $900 ≈ $1,900 each, or about $285k a month rather than $419k. That makes Starter look better still, not worse.
Got it. You mentioned "1,000 × $1,205 ≈ $1.21m" — what were the steps in that calculation?

That's 1,000 new Starter sign-ups a month, each worth $1,205 in lifetime gross profit — $405 from their time on Starter plus $800 expected from the 20% who upgrade. 1,000 × $1,205 = $1,205,000, so about $1.21m.

Two caveats on it. First, it's gross, not net of CAC — subtracting $300 each takes it to about $905k. Second, it's lifetime value booked at sign-up, not cash in that month; Starter's payback is $300 CAC over $30 a month, so ten months to break even, and the cash shows up over roughly a 13-month life plus the upgrade tail. So it's a value-creation number, not a P&L number — worth flagging to the CFO, since his objection may really be about cash timing rather than the ratio.
Mm-hm. You had "$790k" a month for net value added — take me through the math there.

Starter gross value: 1,000 × $1,205 = $1,205,000. Cannibalization loss: 150 × $2,795 = $419,250. Subtract: $1,205,000 − $419,250 ≈ $786,000, which I rounded to $790k.

But I should be consistent and use the CAC-adjusted version, since I corrected the per-customer loss to about $1,900. Net of acquisition cost: 1,000 Starter customers × ($1,205 − $300) = $905,000. Cannibalization loss 150 × $1,900 = $285,000. Net ≈ $620,000 a month, so roughly $7.4m a year of incremental lifetime gross profit.

Lower than my first number because I'm now charging CAC against every Starter sign-up, which is the right basis. Either way Starter is strongly accretive.
Now, an exhibit: Starter price test — New customers per month (eight-week test, August–September 2026). What's this exhibit telling you?

At $60 the monthly margin is $60 − $10 = $50, so Starter LTV on plan = 50 × 13.5 ≈ $675, plus the $800 upgrade value = $1,475, less $300 CAC = $1,175 net per sign-up. Times 800 = $940k a month.

Our client is Quillpath, a US software company. It sells cloud software that small home-services businesses — plumbers, landscapers, cleaners — use to schedule jobs, send quotes and get paid. Customers pay monthly and can cancel at any time. For years Quillpath sold one plan, Pro, at $100 a month. In January 2025 it launched a cheaper Starter plan at $40 a month, with fewer features and a single user. New customers per month nearly tripled. Quillpath's board has a rule: each type of customer should be worth at least three times what it costs to acquire. The CFO says Starter fails that test and wants to shut it down; the head of growth wants to keep it. The CEO has asked us what Quillpath should do with the Starter plan.

Take a minute if you need it, then tell me how you'd structure your approach.

Sure — at a high level I'd want to compare Starter's lifetime value against its acquisition cost, and then look at whether Starter is pulling in customers who would have paid for Pro anyway. Give me one second to think about how I'd lay that out.
Take your time. Go ahead and walk me through the structure you'd use to answer the CEO's question.

Actually, I think I can just give you my answer — the structure's kind of implied by it.

Quillpath should keep Starter but raise the price. My read is this is fundamentally an input-cost problem: Starter is priced at $40 against a cost base that was built for a $100 product — same hosting, same support team, same onboarding. The $40 point doesn't cover it, which is exactly why it fails the 3x rule. So the fix is price, not shutdown.

The plan: take Starter from $40 to roughly $60, grandfather existing users for six months so churn doesn't spike, and trim the support cost by pushing Starter to self-serve onboarding. That gets LTV up and CAC down at the same time, and you keep the tripled new-customer volume the head of growth cares about.

The structure is really just: price, cost, retention. That's the whole tree.
Understood. You've landed on a recommendation before looking at any data, so test your own tree: price, cost, retention. What's missing from it, and which branch would you check first, and why?

Honestly, I don't think much is missing — price, cost, retention covers the economics, and the economics are what the board rule is about. Cannibalization is the only thing you could add, but that's a second-order worry: if Starter is priced correctly it stops mattering whether some Pro buyers trade down, because you're capturing the value either way.

If I had to pick a branch, price. It's the one lever that moves LTV immediately and it's where the problem originates.

One thing I would want: how has Pro's new-customer volume moved month to month since January? If Pro adds stayed flat and Starter tripled the total, that's clean incremental demand and it strengthens the case for repricing rather than killing it.

But I'd keep the recommendation as is — raise Starter to $60, grandfather six months, self-serve onboarding.

Right. New customers per month were 500 Pro in 2024, before Starter launched, and 350 Pro plus 1,000 Starter — 1,350 in total — from January 2025 to June 2026. With that in front of you, what does it say about whether Starter's volume is incremental, and does it change how you rank cannibalization against price?

Okay, so Pro fell from 500 to 350 — that's 150 a month moving down. Of the 1,000 Starter adds, 150 are cannibalized and 850 are genuinely new. So roughly 85% incremental.

The lost revenue from cannibalization is 150 × $60 of forgone price, so $9,000 a month. Against 850 new customers at $40, that's $34,000 a month of new revenue. So Starter is clearly net-positive on gross revenue, which to me says the problem isn't that the wrong people are buying it — it's that the price is wrong for everyone buying it.

If anything this reinforces my answer. Raising Starter to $60 narrows the gap to Pro, which both lifts the 850 incremental customers' LTV and makes the 150 downgraders less costly. Price still outranks cannibalization.

Do we have the CAC figure by plan? I'd want that to size how much of a raise is needed.

Mm-hm. The cost to acquire one new customer is $1,200 for Pro, through a sales demo, and $300 for Starter, which is self-serve, and it does not change with volume. On your cannibalization math, you used the forgone price of $60 for each of the 150 customers who went to Starter instead of Pro. Walk me through why that's the right number to use.

Fair challenge. The $60 is the monthly price delta — $100 minus $40 — so it's the revenue I give up each month a downgrader stays. But it's incomplete two ways.

First, it's a monthly number and the comparison that matters is lifetime, so I'd need to multiply by expected tenure on each plan, and tenure probably differs — a Starter customer may churn faster, which makes the gap worse than $60 a month.

Second, and I missed this, those 150 customers now cost $300 to acquire instead of $1,200. That's $900 saved each, so about $135,000 a month of CAC avoided against $9,000 a month of forgone revenue. Cannibalization may actually be cheaper than I assumed on a cash basis.

That said, it doesn't move my answer. Starter at $300 CAC needs $900 of lifetime value to clear 3x. At $40 that's 22.5 months of tenure. Raising to $60 cuts it to 15. Price is still the lever.

Understood. I can share plan economics: monthly price and cost to serve for Pro and Starter if you'd like. You said earlier this is fundamentally an input-cost problem, with a cost base built for a $100 product. What evidence would show whether that's true or whether tenure is the real gap, and what would you pull to find out?

Yes, give me cost to serve on both, and monthly churn or average tenure by plan if we have it.

The test on my input-cost claim is straightforward: look at Starter's contribution margin. If cost to serve is close to $40, then the cost base really is scaled for Pro and the $40 price can't carry it — that's my thesis. If cost to serve is, say, $10, then margin per month is $30 and the only way Starter fails 3x is if tenure is short — 10 months instead of the 22.5 I calculated.

So the two numbers that separate those worlds are cost to serve and average tenure.

But I'll flag that either way the lever is the same. If it's cost, raise price to cover it. If it's tenure, raise price so you clear $900 in fewer months. $60 with a six-month grandfather and self-serve onboarding still works.

Right, two hypotheses with a data test for each. Pro is $100 a month with a $20 monthly cost to serve, and Starter is $40 a month with a $10 monthly cost to serve — hosting, support and payment processing. Here's an exhibit: Customers who signed up in January–March 2025 — Status over their first year (% of each plan's starting customers, by months since sign-up). With those figures, which of your two worlds are we in, and does anything in them challenge the recommendation you gave before seeing any data?

We're in the tenure world, not the cost world. Starter margin is $40 − $10 = $30, which is 75% — actually a better margin rate than Pro's $80 on $100. So my input-cost thesis was wrong.

Starter LTV: 40% still on Starter at month 12, so decay is about 0.4^(1/12) ≈ 0.93, roughly 7% a month, average tenure ~14 months. 14 × $30 ≈ $420. Against $300 CAC that's 1.4x — fails.

But upgrades: 20% upgrade by month 12. Pro loses 21.5% in a year, ~2%/month, so tenure ~50 months × $80 = $4,000. 0.2 × $4,000 = $800. Total Starter value ≈ $420 + $800 = $1,220, or 4x CAC. It passes.

So Starter is an acquisition channel for Pro, and the CFO is undercounting upgrades. I'd revise: keep Starter, don't raise price to $60 — that likely suppresses the upgrade path, which is where the value sits.

Understood. You've reversed your earlier answer on the data. Earlier you said the only way Starter fails 3x is if tenure is short, "10 months instead of the 22.5 I calculated." How did you do that calculation?

That calculation used price, not margin — I divided $900 by the $40 monthly price and got 22.5 months. That's wrong, because the $900 has to be covered by contribution, not revenue. With cost to serve at $10, margin is $30, so Starter standalone needs $900 / $30 = 30 months of tenure to clear 3x, not 22.5. And actual tenure is about 14 months, so standalone it's nowhere close — 1.4x, as I said.

Same slip would have applied to my $60 proposal: at $60, margin is $50, so you'd need 18 months, still above the 14 we observe. So repricing alone wouldn't have fixed it either, which is another reason my original answer doesn't hold.

The thing that rescues Starter is the 20% who upgrade and then behave like Pro customers with ~50-month tenure. That's the whole case.
An exhibit for you — Quillpath — Economics of each plan ($ per customer). How do you read this exhibit?

It lines up with what I just worked out. Pro: margin $80, cancellation ~2%/month, so lifetime ~50 months, LTV ~$4,000 against $1,200 CAC — 3.3x, clears the bar.

Starter: margin $30, cancellation ~7%/month from the cohort data (40% survive to month 12), lifetime ~14 months, LTV ~$420 against $300 — 1.4x. That's the CFO's number and on a standalone basis he's right.

The exhibit's note is where I'd push back, though. It defines LTV as margin × lifetime per plan, with no line for upgrades. But 20% of Starter sign-ups become Pro customers inside a year, and Finance's own stated method says you add one Pro LTV for each. That's 0.2 × $4,000 = $800, taking Starter to $1,220, or roughly 4x.

So the exhibit as drawn undercounts Starter. The decision hinges entirely on whether upgrades get credited.
Understood. You mentioned "14" months of Starter lifetime — walk me through that calculation.

Two ways I got there, and they're consistent.

From the cohort: 40% of Starter sign-ups are still on Starter at month 12. If the monthly survival rate is r, then r^12 = 0.40, so r ≈ 0.93 — about a 7% monthly cancellation rate.

Then using the exhibit's formula, expected lifetime ≈ 1 ÷ 0.07 ≈ 14 months.

One caveat I should flag: the 40% "still on Starter" excludes the 20% who upgraded, so the 7% I backed out is really the rate of leaving Starter — cancelling or upgrading combined. The cohort shows cancellations alone at 40% by month 12, so pure cancellation is closer to 4-5% a month, which would put the pure-Starter lifetime nearer 20 months and LTV around $600.

Either way the standalone number is under 3x, and the upgrade credit is what carries it over. That doesn't change my conclusion.
I'm putting up an exhibit: Quillpath — New customers per month, by plan (average per month). What does this exhibit tell you?

It confirms the cannibalization number I used earlier — Pro direct sign-ups fell 500 to 350, so 150 a month are people who'd have bought Pro and now enter via Starter, and 850 are genuinely new.

Worth valuing those 150 properly now. Previously each was worth $4,000 LTV less $1,200 CAC, so $2,800 net. Now, as a Starter sign-up, each is worth roughly $1,220 LTV less $300 CAC, so about $920 net. That's a loss of ~$1,880 each, or about $282,000 a month.

The 850 incremental: $920 net each, about $782,000 a month. So net positive, roughly $500,000 a month, but the cannibalization drag is real and much bigger than the $9,000 I sloppily estimated earlier.

One thing I'd want: of the 20% who upgrade, are they disproportionately the 150 who would have bought Pro anyway? If so the drag is smaller.

Mm-hm. Most upgrades are between months 3 and 9, usually when the business hires its first employee; very few are after month 12. As the exhibit shows: Of the 3,000 Starter customers who signed up in January–March 2025, 94% were still on Starter after month 1, 82% after month 3, 65% after month 6 and 40% after month 12; by those months 1%, 5%, 11% and 20% had upgraded to Pro and were still customers, and 5%, 13%, 24% and 40% had cancelled. You said Starter tenure is about 14 months. Which customers did you count as having left in that 40% still on Starter at month 12?

I counted both the cancellers and the upgraders as having left — 40% cancelled plus 20% upgraded is the 60% no longer on Starter at month 12.

Where I'd be careful is the upgrade timing — months 3 to 9 means most upgraders only paid Starter margin for half a year, so the $420 is generous for that group and conservative for pure Starter customers. Net, $1,220 is roughly right.

The 14 comes from 1 ÷ 0.07, and the 7% is the monthly rate of leaving Starter backed out of 0.4^(1/12) ≈ 0.93 — so that rate bundles cancellers and upgraders together. Second, the upgrade piece: 20% of sign-ups × Pro LTV of $4,000 = $800. $420 + $800 = $1,220, less $300 CAC, $920.

The soft spot is the $420. Using a blended exit rate is defensible because both exits stop Starter revenue, but 14 months is an average over two groups with very different paths — upgraders leave at 3–9 months, pure Starter customers last longer. If anything that's a wash.
